source_text: Dixi quid debeatur deo: dicam nunc quid homini tribuendum sit; quamquam id ipsum quod homini tribueris, deo tribuitur, quia homo dei simulacrum est. sed tamen primum iustitiae officium est coniungi cum deo, secundum, cum homine. set illut primum religio dicitur, hoc secundum misericordia uel humanitas nominatur. quae uirtus propria est iustorum et cultorum dei, quod ea sola uitae communis continet rationem. deus enim qui ceteris animalibus sapientiam non dedit, naturalibus ea munimentis ab incursu et periculo tutiora generauit, hominem uero quia nudum fragilemque formauit, ut eum sapientia potius instrueret, dedit ei praeter cetera hunc pietatis adfectum, ut homo hominem tueatur diligat foueat contraque omnia pericula et accipiat et praestet auxilium. summum igitur inter se hominum uinculum est humanitas: quod qui diruperit, nefarius et parricida existimandus est. nam si ab uno homine quem deus finxit omnes orimur, certe consanguinei sumus et ideo maximum scelus putandum est odisse hominem uel nocentem. propterea deus praecepit inimicitias per nos numquam faciendas, semper esse tollendas, scilicet ut eos qui sint nobis inimici necessitudinis admonitos mitigemus. item si ab uno deo mspirati omnes et animati sumus, quid aliut quam fratres sumus, et quidem coniunctiores, quod animis, quam qui corporibus ? itaque non errat Lucretius, cum dicit: denique caelesti sumus omnes semine oriundi, omnibus ille idem pater est . ergo pro beluis inmanibus sunt habendi qui homini nocent, qui contra IUS humanitatis et fas omne spoliant cruciant occidunt exterminant. ob hanc necessitudinem germanitatis docet nos deus malum numquam facere, semper bonum. id autem ipsum bene facere quid sit, idem ipse praescribit: praestare auxilium depressis et laborantibus, inpertiri uictum non habentibus. deus enim quoniam pius est, animal nos uoluit esse sociale: itaque in aliis hominibus nos ipsos cogitare debemus. non meremur in periculo liberari, si non succurrimus, non meremur auxilium, si negamus. ad hanc partem philosophorum nulla praecepta sunt, quippe qui falsae uirtutis specie capti misericordiam de homine sustulerunt et dum uolunt sanare, uitiauerunt. et cum idem plerumque fateantur societatis humanae communionem esse retinendam, ab ea plane se ipsos inhumanae uirtutis suae rigore dissociant. conuincendus ergo etiam hic error illorum est qui nihil cuiquam inpertiendum putant. urbis condendae originem atque causam non unam intulerunt, sed alii eos homines qui sint ex terra primitus nati, cum per siluas et campos erraticam degerent uitam, nec ullo inter se sermonis aut iuris uinculo cohaererent, sed frondes et herbam pro cubilibus, speluncas et antra pro domibus haberent, bestiis et fortioribus animalibus praedae fuisse commemorant. tum eos qui aut laniati effugerant aut laniari proximos uiderant, admonitos periculi sui ad alios homines decucurrisse, praesidium inplorasse et primo nutibus uoluntatem suam significasse, deinde sermonis initia temptasse ac singulis quibusque rebus nomina inprimendo paulatim loquendi perfecisse rationem. cum autem multitudinem ipsam uiderent contra bestias esse tutandam, oppida etiam coepisse munire, ut uel quietem noctis tutam sibi facerent uel ut incursiones atque impetus bestiarum non pugnando, sed obiectis aggeribus arcerent. o ingenia hominibus indigna, quae has ineptias protulerunt, miseros atque miserabiles, qui stultitiam suam litteris memoriaeque mandauerint ! qui cum uiderent mutis quoque animalibus ingenitam esse rationem uel conueniendi uel inuicem adpetendi uel periculi fugiendi uel mali cauendi uel cubilia sibi et latibula parandi, homines tamen ipsos existimauerint non nisi exemplis admoneri ac discere potuisse, quid metuere, quid cauere, quid facere deberent, aut numquam conuenturos inter se fuisse nec loquendi rationem reperturos, nisi eos bestiae comedissent. haec aliis delira uisa sunt, ut fuerunt, dixeruntque non ferarum laniatus causam fuisse coeundi, sed ipsam potius humanitatem, itaque inter se congregatos, quod natura hominum solitudinis fugiens et communionis ac societatis adpetens esset. non magna inter eos disceptatio est, siquidem causae dispares sunt, res eadem est. potuit igitur utrumque, quia non repugnat, sed tamen utrumque nullo modo uerum est, quia non per omnem terram nati sunt homines e terra tamquam ex draconis alicuius dentibus proseminati, ut poetae ferunt, sed unus homo a deo fictus ab eoque uno terra omnis humano genere conpleta est, eadem scilicet ratione qua rursus post diluuium; quod certe negare non possunt. nulla igitur in principio facta est eiusmodi congregatio nec umquam fuisse homines in terra qui praeter infantiam non loquerentur, intelleget cui ratio non deest. fingamus tamen illa uera esse quae otiosi et inepti senes fabulantur, ut eos suis potissimum sensibus et suis rationibus refellamus. si hac de causa sunt homines congregati, ut mutuis auxiliis inbecillitatem suam tuerentur, succurrendum est igitur homini qui egeat auxilio. cum enim praesidii causa homines societatem cum hominibus inierint et sanxerint., foedus illut a principio sui ortus inter homines tutum aut uiolare aut non conseruare summum nefas putandum est. nam qui se a praestando auxilio remouet, etiam ab accipiendo remoueat necesse est, quia nullius opera indigere se putat qui alteri suam denegat. huic uero, qui se ipse dissociat ac secernit a corpore, non ritu hominis, sed ferarum more uiuendum est. quod si fieri non potest, retinendum igitur omni modo uinculum societatis humanae, quia homo sine homine nullo modo potest uiuere. retentio autem societatis est communitas, id est auxilium praestare, ut possimus accipere. sin uero, ut illi alii disputant, humanitatis ipsius causa facta est hominum congregatio, homo certe hominem debet adgnoscere. quod si fecerunt illi rudes et adhuc fen homines et fecerunt nondum constituta loquendi ratione, quid putemus hominibus expolitis et sermonis rerumque omnium commercio inter se copulatis esse faciendum, qui adsueti hominibus solitudinem ferre non possunt?
pass_a_gloss: What you give a human you give God, for the human is God's image. First justice joins to God — religion; second to the human — mercy or humanity, the virtue of the just and of God's worshipers. Philosophers, captivated by a false look of virtue, tore mercy from the human. If humans gathered for mutual help or for humanity itself, aid must be given to the needy; to break that bond is to live like beasts — a human cannot live without a human.
pass_b_english: I have said what is owed to God: I will now say what is to be granted to a human; although that very thing which you have granted to a human is granted to God, because a human is God's image. But still the first office of justice is to be joined with God, the second with a human. But that first is called religion, this second is named mercy or humanity. Which virtue is proper to the just and to the worshipers of God, because it alone holds the reason of common life. For God, who did not give wisdom to the other animals, generated them safer by natural defenses from assault and danger; but a human, because he shaped him naked and fragile that he might rather equip him with wisdom, gave him besides the rest this affection of piety, that human may guard, love, foster human and against all dangers both receive and offer help. The highest bond therefore among humans is humanity: which who has broken must be thought wicked and a murderer. For if we all arise from one human whom God fashioned, we are certainly of one blood and therefore it must be thought the greatest crime to hate a human even when harmful. For that reason God commanded enmities never to be made by us, always to be removed, namely that we may soften those who are enemies to us when reminded of kinship. Likewise if we all are inspired and given life by one God, what else are we than brothers, and indeed more closely joined because by souls than those who by bodies? And so Lucretius does not err when he says: 'Finally we all are sprung from heavenly seed; that same one is father to all.' Therefore they are to be held for wild beasts who harm a human, who against the right of humanity and every divine law strip, torture, kill, exile. For this kinship of brotherhood God teaches us never to do evil, always good. But what it itself is to do good, he himself also prescribes: to offer help to the pressed and laboring, to impart food to those not having. For God since he is pious willed us to be a social animal: and so in other humans we ought to think of ourselves. We do not deserve to be freed in danger if we do not help, we do not deserve help if we refuse.

Toward this part the philosophers have no precepts, inasmuch as captivated by the appearance of false virtue they have removed mercy from the human and while they will to heal have spoiled. And though the same often confess that the fellowship of human society is to be kept, by the rigidity of their inhuman virtue they plainly dissociate themselves from it. This error of theirs also must therefore be convicted who think nothing should be imparted to anyone. They have brought in not one origin and cause of founding a city, but some recount that those humans who were first born from earth, when they spent a wandering life through woods and fields and cohered by no bond of speech or right among themselves, but had leaves and grass for beds, caves and dens for homes, were prey to beasts and stronger animals. Then those who had either escaped torn or had seen neighbors torn, warned of their danger, ran down to other humans, begged protection and first by nods signified their will, then tried the beginnings of speech and by impressing names on each several things gradually completed the system of speaking. And when they saw the multitude itself must be guarded against beasts, they also began to fortify towns, that they might either make the rest of night safe for themselves or keep off the rushes and assaults of beasts not by fighting but by thrown-up mounds. O talents unworthy of humans, which have put forward these sillinesses, wretched and pitiable, who have committed their folly to letters and memory! Who when they saw that even to mute animals reason is inborn either of gathering or of seeking one another or of fleeing danger or of guarding against evil or of preparing beds and dens for themselves, still thought humans themselves could not be warned and learn except by examples what they ought to fear, guard against, do, or that they would never have met among themselves nor found a system of speaking unless beasts had eaten them. These things seemed delirious to others, as they were, and they said not the tearing of wild beasts was the cause of gathering, but rather humanity itself, and so they were gathered among themselves because humans' nature flees solitude and seeks fellowship and society.

There is not a great dispute among them, since the causes are different, the thing is the same. Both therefore could be, because it does not conflict, but still both is by no means true, because humans were not born through all the earth from earth as if sown from some dragon's teeth, as the poets say, but one human was fashioned by God and from that one all the earth was filled with the human race, by the same reason clearly as again after the flood; which certainly they cannot deny. No gathering of that sort therefore was made in the beginning nor were there ever humans on earth who beyond infancy did not speak, he will understand to whom reason is not lacking. But let us suppose those things true which idle and silly old men invent, that we may refute them by their own senses and reasons. If for this cause humans were gathered, that by mutual helps they might guard their weakness, help must therefore be given to a human who needs help. For since for the sake of protection humans have entered society with humans and have sanctioned it, to violate that covenant from the beginning of its birth among humans or not to keep it must be thought the highest crime. For who removes himself from offering help must also necessarily remove himself from receiving, because he thinks he needs no one's work who denies his own to another. But for this one who dissociates and separates himself from the body, one must live not by human rite but by beasts' custom. Which if it cannot happen, the bond of human society must therefore be kept in every way, because a human without a human can by no means live. But keeping of society is community, that is to offer help that we may be able to receive. But if, as those others argue, the gathering of humans was made for the sake of humanity itself, a human ought certainly to acknowledge a human. Which if those rude and still almost wild humans did, and did it with the system of speaking not yet established, what should we think must be done by polished humans joined among themselves by commerce of speech and of all things, who accustomed to humans cannot bear solitude?

lemmas.gloss: justice: religion toward God, mercy toward humans
what you give a human you give God; human is God's image
humanity's bond is mutual help; without a human none lives

rejected: justice is only cult toward God
choices.why: First office joins to God (religion); second to the human (mercy).

rejected: aid to humans is secular and godless
choices.why: Aid to a human is given to God, because the human is God's image.
Society's bond is mutual help; refusing aid breaks humanity and lives like a beast.
